source.quote: Problem definition: We consider contract confidentiality in a decentralized supply chain, in which a single principal orders different components from different agents, each of which has private cost information.

Problem definition: We consider contract confidentiality in a decentralized supply chain, in which a single principal orders different components from different agents, each of which has private cost information.
With NDAs or secret contracting/offers, a supplier does not observe the contractual terms offered to other suppliers (i.e., each contract menu is not publicly com­ mitted).

Building on the seminal work of Hart and Tirole (1990), subsequent research concentrates on the settings of an upstream firm (principal) and competing down­ stream firms (agents); see pioneering works by O’Brien and Shaffer (1992), McAfee and Schwartz (1994), Segal (1999), and Segal and Whinston (2003).

The crux of the problem of secrecy is as follows: in any contract that results in a vertically integrated outcome, both the principal and any agent can increase their bilateral profits by pri­ vately negotiating a reduction in their marginal transfer and retail price, which would divert customers and profits from rival agents.

Problem definition: We consider contract confidentiality in a decentralized supply chain, in which a single principal orders different components from different agents, each of which has private cost information.

However, in a scenario in which the agents pro­ vide perfectly complementary products, secret offers remove their synchronization of perspectives in the total wholesale price, but it is still in the best interest of each agent for the other to receive the optimal output quantity.

Sequential Contracting The timeline of sequential contracting goes as follows. (1) The principal offers a contract menu, (W1(·),T1(·)), to agent 1. (2) Agent 1 chooses a contract from the menu. (3) The principal offers a contract menu, (W2(·|c1), t2(·|c1)), to agent 2. (4) Agent 2 chooses a contract from the menu. (5) Based on the two agents’ choices, the principal makes a decision on input orders from each agent and follows through the sale.

Recent works expanding on these include Gaudin (2019), Rey and Verg´e (2019), and Do and Mikl´os-Thal (2020) along with Dequiedt and Martimort (2015) and Pagnozzi et al. (2021) exploring private information among agents, an aspect also considered in our study.

conditions: Comparing the secrecy program (see (15)) with the publicity program (see Program P in (24)), passive beliefs add an additional requirement to the principal’s optimization problem: agents’ beliefs must be consistent with the equilibrium.

To understand the intuition behind the distinction between the two scenarios, note that moving from the public-offer scenario to the secret-offer scenario resembles the transition from trilateral to bilateral negotiation, which is the crux of how secrecy influences vertical contracting decisions (O’Brien and Shaffer 1992).

More specifically, in the public-offer scenario, the total wholesale price can be optimized by the principal as a single decision variable because the agents are committed to the total wholesale price (see program P in (24)).
